title: With Due Respect (Vol. 1) -- Ch. 7: Will GMA Win the Cha-cha War?
keywords: Will GMA Win the Cha-cha War?
Let the people be the judge
primary_topics: Chapter 7 of 'With Due Respect' (Vol. 1) -- CJP's July 27, 2008 Inquirer column (a sequel to 'Can GMA Reign Beyond 2010?') handicapping whether GMA could win a parliamentary-shift 'Cha-cha war' and, 'unlike Ferdinand Marcos,' do it 'without martial law'

The Marcos precedent: how, after declaring martial law in 1972, Marcos got an obliging Constitutional Convention to approve the 1973 Constitution shifting to a parliamentary form and extending his rule -- a 'wily lawyer' cloaking iron rule in 'constitutional authoritarianism' with the backing of the military and the United States

A political map of the contest: the presidential 'wannabes' and oppositionists arrayed against GMA, the militants/civil-society/business/media 'political noise,' and -- the decisive 'swing group' -- the 'middle forces' (bishops, Catholic laity, El Shaddai) who would be galvanized by 'bread and butter' issues

Why martial law cannot save GMA as it saved Marcos -- the 1987 Charter 'extracted the teeth of martial law' (invasion or rebellion only, a 60-day cap, no suspension of habeas corpus or of the Constitution, Court and Congress) -- so that if the 'enraged middle forces' fill the streets during the Con-ass debates, GMA's allies 'may just bugle an early retreat'
sub_topics: The framing questions (carried over): will Congress, the Court, the Comelec and the people let GMA stay past June 30, 2010, and can she -- unlike Marcos -- extend her reign 'without martial law'?

The Marcos precedent: with the 1971 Con-con disinclined to extend his term (ending December 1973), Marcos declared martial law on September 21, 1972, after which the Con-con 'obligingly' approved the 1973 Constitution shifting to a parliamentary form and extending his rule indefinitely

Marcos the legalist: a 'wily lawyer' and 'stickler for legalism,' he boasted that Proclamation 1081 was issued 'pursuant to' the then Constitution and branded his regime 'constitutional authoritarianism,' knowing the military and the international community (especially the US) would back a 'veneer of constitutional legitimacy'

GMA's likely route and opponents: she would choose the constituent assembly (Con-ass), but the presidential 'wannabes' (Estrada, Lacson, Legarda, Roxas, Villar) and oppositionists (Binay, the Cayetanos, Escudero, Madrigal, Pimentel) would 'besiege her,' with militants, party-lists, civil society, labor, business (the Makati Business Club) and students adding 'political noise' and the media intensifying attacks

The swing group -- the 'middle forces': those who, to preserve the democratic institutions, were willing to wait out GMA's term but would now face 'the specter of her continued stay' -- including bishops, Catholic laity and El Shaddai -- mobilized by 'bread and butter' issues (soaring food/transport/fuel/energy prices, deteriorating peace and order, corruption)

GMA's weapons: government resources and her political machinery (the 'Lakas-Kampi monolith,' her grip on the House and on governors, mayors and barangay leaders); a master of patronage who 'dispenses' the budget, PAGCOR/PCSO funds, infrastructure, and VAT 'katas' (low-cost rice, lifeline electricity); the controversial JELAC meeting in the Court's 'inner sanctum' where she committed a 'P3-billion largesse for the judiciary'; choice appointees to the Court and Comelec and a network of generals

The Marcos parallel and its limit: Marcos too had 'political sycophants, friendly justices, compliant election officials and fat pork barrels' -- but the 1987 Charter 'extracted the teeth of martial law,' allowing it only for 'invasion or rebellion,' for a period 'not exceeding 60 days,' without suspending the writ of habeas corpus or the operation of the Constitution, the Court and Congress

The verdict: quoting Executive Secretary Ermita's mantra, 'Let the people be the judge' -- 'provided the Comelec counts the votes accurately'; and if the 'enraged middle forces' pour into the streets during the Con-ass debates, the 'Cha-cha express' may never reach the Court, the Comelec and the plebiscite, and GMA's allies 'may just bugle an early retreat'

notable_anecdotes: 'Constitutional authoritarianism': CJP recalls that Marcos, 'the wily lawyer,' boasted that Proclamation 1081 was issued 'pursuant to' the Constitution and branded his martial-law regime with that phrase to keep the military and the US on side.

The P3-billion in the inner sanctum: he flags the 'unprecedented' JELAC meeting held 'right in the Supreme Court's inner sanctum,' where GMA committed a 'P3-billion largesse for the judiciary' -- patronage reaching even the courts.
VAT 'katas': he describes how GMA justifies VAT 'as a tax on the rich' and dispenses its 'katas' as low-cost NEA rice, lifeline electricity subsidies and other doles -- patronage perfected.

The toothless martial law: against the Marcos parallel, he itemizes how the 1987 Charter limits martial law -- invasion or rebellion only, 60 days maximum, and no suspension of the writ or of the Constitution, Court and Congress -- so it 'may not help GMA the way it did Marcos.'

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 7 of 'With Due Respect' (Vol. 1), CJP's July 27, 2008 Inquirer column and a sequel to 'Can GMA Reign Beyond 2010?', handicaps whether GMA could win a parliamentary-shift 'Cha-cha war' and, 'unlike Ferdinand Marcos,' do it 'without martial law.' He recalls the Marcos precedent: with the 1971 Constitutional Convention disinclined to extend his term, Marcos declared martial law in September 1972, after which the Con-con 'obligingly' approved the 1973 Constitution shifting to a parliamentary form and extending his rule -- the 'wily lawyer' cloaking iron rule in 'constitutional authoritarianism' with the backing of the military and the United States. Turning to the present, he maps the field arrayed against a GMA constituent-assembly push: the presidential 'wannabes' (Estrada, Lacson, Legarda, Roxas, Villar) and oppositionists, the militants, civil society, business and media 'political noise,' and -- the decisive 'swing group' -- the 'middle forces' (bishops, Catholic laity, El Shaddai) who, mobilized by 'bread and butter' issues, become 'a march of the hungry and the angry' that 'would be invincible.' Against this he weighs GMA's 'weapons' -- the Lakas-Kampi machinery, her grip on the House and local officials, and a perfected patronage that dispenses the budget, PAGCOR/PCSO funds, infrastructure and VAT 'katas,' even a 'P3-billion largesse for the judiciary' pledged at a JELAC meeting in the Court's 'inner sanctum.' But, he argues, Marcos too had sycophants, friendly justices and compliant officials; the crucial difference is that the 1987 Charter 'extracted the teeth of martial law' -- allowing it only for 'invasion or rebellion,' for 'not exceeding 60 days,' and without suspending the writ of habeas corpus or the operation of the Constitution, the Court and Congress -- so martial law 'may not help GMA the way it did Marcos.' Quoting Ermita's 'Let the people be the judge' (provided the Comelec counts accurately), he concludes that if the enraged middle forces fill the streets during the Con-ass debates, the 'Cha-cha express' may never reach the Court, the Comelec and the plebiscite, and GMA's allies 'may just bugle an early retreat.'
